strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: pinpointing decisive errors in multi-agent system trajectories, which is costly to debug manually.

The core idea—that MAS failures recur with structurally similar patterns that can be distilled into compact, reusable 'schemas' rather than replayed as raw few-shot exemplars—is intuitive and empirically motivated (Figures 1-3 show naive ICL fails due to context length and noise).

Extensive experimentation across many model families (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek) and both the WHO&WHEN benchmark and the newly introduced CORRECT-Error benchmark, with consistent, often substantial relative improvements over LLM-as-a-judge, fine-tuning, and naive ICL baselines.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations: schema cache size, number of retrieved schemas, cross-dataset/cross-model schema transferability, and comparison to an oracle schema upper bound, which together support the claim that a small number of distilled schemas captures most recurring error structure.

CORRECT-Error is a useful contribution: over 2,000 annotated trajectories across seven diverse tasks, an order of magnitude larger than prior human-annotated resources, produced via an interesting bootstrap error-injection pipeline and validated with a dedicated human study showing synthetic errors are largely indistinguishable from real ones.
Additional finding that LLM agents have poor self-recognition of their own injected errors (Figure 11) is a useful complementary insight motivating the need for external detection tools.
weaknesses: Despite relative gains of up to ~20 points, absolute exact-step accuracy remains very low in many settings (e.g., 17.2% Acc@0 for the strongest model, GPT-5, on Human-Crafted data), raising questions about the practical readiness of the method for real deployment despite the framing of 'near-zero overhead' automated recognition.

Potential circularity/leakage concerns: GPT-5 is used both to generate/inject synthetic errors in CORRECT-Error (matching successful trajectories to their closest human-labeled error trajectory and adapting the pattern) and later as the schema generator/detector evaluated on that same benchmark; this could bias results in favor of GPT-5-based schema extraction and make synthetic errors artificially easier to match against schemas derived from similar seed patterns.

The number of retrieved schemas (a key hyperparameter) was tuned directly on the evaluation datasets themselves (Appendix A.1: chosen via experiments on Hand-Crafted, Algorithm-Generated, and HotpotQA, then fixed for all other datasets/models) without a clear held-out validation split, which risks overfitting the reported numbers to the specific test sets.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat uneven: fine-tuning and naive ICL baselines are only evaluated with the small Qwen-2.5-7B model, not with the stronger closed-source models used for CORRECT, making it hard to assess whether the reported advantage would hold against stronger fine-tuned or ICL-augmented systems.

No experiments directly evaluate the 'dynamic schema management' (expansion/distillation) component described in Algorithm 1, despite it being presented as a core part of the framework; the online adaptivity claim is therefore unverified empirically.

Variance/statistical significance is not reported despite averaging over five runs, and some oracle comparisons show CORRECT nominally exceeding oracle performance (104%), which is not explained and raises concern about measurement noise or evaluation protocol issues.

The claim of being 'training-free' and low-cost is in tension with the reported cost of the data/schema generation pipeline (over 3 billion GPT-5/GPT-4o tokens), which, while separate from inference-time cost, is a non-trivial resource investment not fully contextualized against fine-tuning alternatives.

Directly relevant recent work (e.g., Ge et al., 2025, spectrum-analysis-based failure attribution) is discussed but not included as an empirical baseline, leaving open whether CORRECT truly represents the current state of the art.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: training-free, lightweight decisive error localization in multi-agent systems, with clear motivation grounded in real deployment constraints (data scarcity, compute cost, dynamic error types).

The core insight—that MAS failures recur with structurally similar patterns and can be distilled into reusable 'error schemata'—is empirically supported by a semantic similarity analysis on WHO&WHEN (>80% of failure trajectories have a high-similarity counterpart), and the naive ICL failure mode is convincingly demonstrated before motivating the schema-based design.

Extensive experimentation: evaluation spans 11+ models (open and closed source), multiple baselines (LLM-as-judge, fine-tuning, ICL, MIPRO), seven downstream tasks, and numerous ablations (cache size, number of schemata, thresholds, retrieval noise, oracle comparison, online streaming adaptation, cross-domain transfer to AgentErrorBench and Cemri et al.'s taxonomy).

Introduces CORRECT-Error, a reasonably large synthetic benchmark (2000+ trajectories) built via a structured bootstrap error-injection pipeline, accompanied by a dedicated human evaluation study (120+ annotator hours) suggesting synthetic and real errors are difficult to distinguish.

Reports practical considerations often omitted in similar papers: near-zero inference/latency overhead, robustness to context truncation, and a downstream 'decisive intervention' experiment showing localization improves actual task recovery rates.
Well-organized algorithmic description (offline extraction, online retrieval, dynamic cache management) with clear formalization of the decisive-error notion following prior work.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracy remains low in most settings (e.g., Acc@0 around 6-17% even with CORRECT on WHO&WHEN), so despite relative gains over weak baselines, the practical utility of exact-step localization is still limited; the headline '19.8%' improvement is a best-case number (GPT-5, algorithm-generated) not representative of the overall trend, and some configurations even show slight regressions (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash Acc@1 -0.8, Gemini-2.5-pro Acc@0 -0.8).

Potential circularity/self-consistency bias in evaluation: CORRECT-Error trajectories are synthesized via LLM-driven error injection, error schemata are also extracted and matched via LLM prompting, and detection is performed by LLMs — leaving open the possibility that gains partly reflect alignment between the synthetic generation process and the schema-matching process rather than genuine transfer to real-world MAS failures.

The human-alignment study, while a nice addition, is not fully conclusive: given the paper's own claim that human annotators in WHO&WHEN disagree >50% of the time on genuine errors, near-random discrimination between synthetic and real trajectories could partly reflect inherent labeling noise/ambiguity rather than strong synthetic realism.
No variance/confidence intervals are reported despite using median of five runs; given several improvements are only a few points, statistical significance is unclear.
Threshold sensitivity analyses (δ, θ_hot) are conducted on a single dataset (ARC) only, limiting confidence that these hyperparameters generalize across domains.

The clustering-based schema number selection (via silhouette score) is described but not rigorously validated against alternative selection strategies, and its practical effect on end results is only indirectly supported through cache-size ablations.

The method's originality is more in application/engineering integration (RAG-style schema caching + LLM-as-judge) than in a fundamentally new algorithmic technique; similar retrieval-augmented or memory-based reasoning ideas exist in other LLM application contexts, and this connection could be discussed more thoroughly to properly contextualize the contribution.

The multi-error trajectory failure case (Appendix A.11) suggests a nontrivial recurring limitation (schema retrieval favoring more 'salient' but non-earliest errors) that is only briefly acknowledged rather than quantified across the dataset.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: fine-grained, decisive error localization in multi-agent systems, which is costly to annotate and hard to solve with existing LLM-as-judge or fine-tuning approaches.
The training-free, cache-based schema retrieval idea is a reasonable and practical systems-oriented contribution that avoids expensive retraining while adapting online.
Extensive experimental coverage across many model families (Qwen, Llama, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek-R1) and two benchmarks (WHO&WHEN and the newly proposed CORRECT-Error).

A reasonably thorough set of ablations: cache size, number of retrieved schemas, oracle-schema upper bound, robustness to retrieval noise, sensitivity to similarity/hotness thresholds, streaming/online adaptation, and cross-benchmark transfer (Cemri et al., AgentErrorBench).
The human-alignment study for the synthetic CORRECT-Error dataset (near-random human classification between synthetic and real trajectories) is a thoughtful attempt to validate data realism.
Overhead analysis (near-zero added latency/cost) supports the practicality claim for online deployment.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracy remains very low even with CORRECT (e.g., 12.1%–17.2% Acc@0 on WHO&WHEN Human-Crafted), which undercuts claims of practical impact for 'reliable MAS deployment' despite large relative percentage-point gains being emphasized in the abstract and throughout.

Baselines appear weak or under-optimized: the fine-tuned LLM baseline is essentially indistinguishable from the zero-shot LLM-as-judge baseline on Human-Crafted data (3.5% both), raising doubts about whether the fine-tuning and naive-ICL comparisons were implemented competitively, which weakens the strength of the claimed superiority of CORRECT.

The CORRECT-Error dataset construction and its own error-schema extraction both heavily rely on GPT-5-generated content (error injection strategy, schema generation, and even judgment), creating potential circularity: schemas distilled by an LLM are used to detect errors injected by the same/similar LLM family, which could inflate reported gains without demonstrating genuine transfer to real, human-caused MAS failures.

Results show large, inconsistent variance across models on the same dataset (e.g., Gemini-2.5-pro shows a slight decrease of -0.8 on Algorithm-Generated while GPT-5 shows +19.8), suggesting sensitivity to model/prompt choice that is not adequately explained, undermining the generality claims.

Key hyperparameters (e.g., the silhouette-based stopping threshold ϵ for clustering, exact θhot/δ selection procedure) are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility despite claims of open-sourcing code/data.

The paper's central motivating claim (>80% of failure trajectories share ≥0.8 BERT cosine similarity) may reflect surface/lexical/template similarity in logs rather than true structural/causal similarity of decisive errors, which is not disentangled or validated further.

The dynamic schema management mechanism (expansion + distillation), a core claimed contribution for online adaptability, is not clearly ablated in isolation; the streaming experiment (Table 3) shows non-monotonic, somewhat erratic accuracy trends (e.g., WikiMQA decreasing then increasing) that are described as 'stable' without deeper analysis.

The known ambiguity of decisive-error ground truth (WHO&WHEN's reported >50% annotator disagreement) is acknowledged but its implications for the reliability of all reported accuracy numbers (including CORRECT's own gains) are not sufficiently addressed with additional agreement/robustness analysis on the ground-truth labels used for evaluation.

No empirical comparison against the directly relevant fine-tuning-based failure attribution baseline (Ge et al., 2025, spectrum analysis) mentioned in related work, despite it being framed as a key competing paradigm.

strengths: The paper identifies a well-motivated and important problem (decisive error localization in MAS) and provides clear empirical evidence for its core premise—that MAS failures recur with similar structural patterns (semantic similarity CDF analysis on WHO&WHEN)—before proposing a solution, which strengthens the causal story behind the method.

The training-free, cache-based schema distillation approach is a sensible and lightweight alternative to both brittle LLM-as-a-judge prompting and expensive fine-tuning, and the paper demonstrates concretely (via ICL failure analysis in Fig 1b) why naive alternatives do not work, motivating the specific design choices in CORRECT.

Extensive ablations are provided: cache size sensitivity, number of retrieved schemas, oracle-schema upper bound, robustness to retrieval noise (hard negatives), sensitivity to hyperparameters (δ, θhot), online/streaming adaptation, and cross-domain/cross-formulation transfer (to Cemri et al. and AgentErrorBench), which collectively give a fairly thorough picture of the method's behavior.

The CORRECT-Error benchmark is a useful contribution addressing a genuine bottleneck (expensive, low-agreement human annotation), and the human-alignment study (labelers near-random at distinguishing synthetic vs. real errors) provides reasonable evidence of synthetic data fidelity.

Overhead/cost analysis (near-negligible latency and API cost increase) supports the practical deployability claims, and a downstream intervention experiment (targeted restart improving success rate 10%→20%) provides some evidence that imperfect localization still yields actionable value.
weaknesses: Absolute accuracy numbers remain low in an absolute sense (e.g., 12–17% Acc@0 on Human-Crafted WHO&WHEN even with CORRECT), and several improvements are marginal or even negative (e.g., +0.7 for Qwen-2.5-7B Acc@0 on Algorithm-Generated, -0.8 for Gemini-2.5-Flash Acc@1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro Acc@0 in Table 1), raising questions about the practical reliability of the method despite headline claims of "up to 19.8%" or "up to 20 points" improvement, which cherry-picks the best-case model/metric.

No variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported despite claiming median-of-five-runs; given how small some improvements are (single-digit percentage points on small evaluation sets, e.g., WHO&WHEN Human-Crafted has only ~58 test trajectories), it is unclear whether reported gains are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The paper's own §2.2 notes annotation disagreement rates exceeding 50% on WHO&WHEN, which undermines confidence in the ground-truth labels used for both training seeds and evaluation, and by extension complicates interpretation of the human-alignment study in §4.2 (labelers' inability to distinguish synthetic from real errors could partly reflect inherent ambiguity in decisive-error labeling generally, rather than purely synthetic realism).

The fine-tuning baseline (single Qwen-2.5-7B model trained via simple SFT) is relatively weak and may not represent state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches (e.g., RL-based or larger-scale supervised approaches), making the comparison against CORRECT's superiority over fine-tuning somewhat unconvincing as a general claim.

The code/dataset link in the abstract is left blank ("Our code is publicly available at:"), and although the paper promises release, this reduces immediate reproducibility verification at submission time.

The failure case discussion (Appendix A.11) is limited to a single qualitative example of multi-error trajectories; no systematic quantification of how often CORRECT's predicted "decisive" step diverges from the true earliest error due to competing later failures is provided, leaving open how often this failure mode occurs in practice.
